clues.label: Ras the Exhorter
clues.text: Ras the Exhorter becoming Ras the Destroyer as a member of the Brotherhood of this novel.
examples: After Dr. Bledsoe expels him from college, this novel's protagonist delivers rousing speeches for the Brotherhood, who oppose Ras the Exhorter.
This novel's protagonist quits the Brotherhood during a riot led by Ras the Exhorter.
The unnamed narrator of this novel is sealed underground following a riot encouraged by the Brotherhood, whose members include Ras the Exhorter.

clues.label: Dr. Bledsoe
clues.text: For taking Mr. Norton to the Golden Day and letting him speak with Jim Trueblood, the protagonist of this novel is kicked out of a college run by Dr. Bledsoe.
examples: In this novel, the protagonist leads a rich trustee to Jim Trueblood's cabin and a seedy bar, causing him to be expelled from college by Dr. Bledsoe.
For taking Mr. Norton to the Golden Day, this character is expelled from an unnamed school by Dr. Bledsoe.
Dr. Bledsoe expels this character after he chauffeurs Mr. Norton, and he is targeted by Ras the Exhorter after joining the Brotherhood.

clues.label: Tod Clifton
clues.text: In this novel, Sambo dolls are sold by a character who "plunges outside history", Tod Clifton.
examples: Jack's glass eye falls out as he decries this novel's protagonist for supporting Tod Clifton, who had been selling Sambo dolls.
Tod Clifton is later shot by the police and Dr. Bledsoe expels the narrator from the school.
Characters in this novel include the aforementioned Tod Clifton, as well as a character who deliberately gives the protagonist bad letters of recommendation, Dr. Bledsoe.

clues.label: Battle Royal
clues.text: The first chapter of this novel describes a "Battle Royal" where black teenage boys fight each other.
examples: That character in this novel wins a college scholarship by fighting in a "Battle Royal."
White men in tuxedos watch as this character grabs fake gold coins on an electrified carpet after being blindfolded and made to fight nine other Black boys at once in a "battle royal."
This character won a scholarship to that school after winning a sadistic "battle royal."

clues.label: Rinehart
clues.text: While incognito, this character is mistaken for a pimp and reverend named Rinehart.
examples: While wearing a dark hat and sunglasses, this novel's protagonist is repeatedly mistaken for Rinehart.

This character recalls his dying grandfather's advice to "overcome 'em with yeses, undermine 'em with grins" after donning a large hat and green sunglasses that make him look like a con man named Rinehart.
This character is frequently mistaken for a gambler, pimp, and reverend named Rinehart.

clues.text: This novel's narrator lives in an underground room lit by 1,369 lightbulbs after a riot led by Ras the Exhorter.
examples: This novel's protagonist describes owning 1,369 light bulbs before participating in a "Battle Royal."
The narrator of this novel's prologue listens to Louis [Lewis] Armstrong's "Black and Blue" on five record players at once in a room illuminated by 1,369 light bulbs.
The protagonist of this novel steals electricity from Monopolated Light and Power using 1,369 light bulbs.

clues.label: Lucius Brockway
clues.text: This novel's protagonist is fired from a paint factory after Lucius Brockway tricks him into destroying a boiler.
examples: Lucius Brockway tricks this book's protagonist into destroying a boiler room after he wanders into a union meeting.
In one scene in this novel, a paint factory boiler explodes while the protagonist was working with Lucius Brockway.
The protagonist of this novel works with Lucius Brockway, with whom he ends up fighting.

clues.label: Sybil
clues.text: The protagonist of this work attempts to get information by visiting Sybil, who instead gets drunk and wants him to rape her.
examples: This novel's protagonist enacts a "yes, agree, and grin" strategy by filling out fake membership cards and seducing Sybil.
The protagonist of this novel writes "Sybil, you were raped by Santa Claus.
At a birthday party, this character is seduced by a woman with a rape fantasy named Sybil.

clues.label: Liberty Paints
clues.text: This character is subject to electroshock therapy after an explosion at his workplace, Liberty Paints.
examples: After the protagonist of this novel leaves his factory job at Liberty Paints, he becomes a spokesperson for the Brotherhood.
After a boiler explosion at a paint factory, a character in this novel undergoes electroshock therapy and realizes he has forgotten his name.
A hospitalization after an accident at the Liberty Paint factory leads to this character receiving electroshock treatment.

clues.label: social equality
clues.text: The narrator of this novel mistakenly says "social equality" rather than "social responsibility" during a speech to a white audience, members of which had previously had him and other black young men blindfolded and forced to pummel each other.
examples: In its first chapter, the protagonist shouts "social equality!" after being forced to repeat the words "social responsiblity" when laughter drowns out his speech.
The protagonist of this novel, who works at Liberty Paints, accidentally mentions "equality" instead of "responsibility" in a speech given after a battle royale with nine of his schoolmates.
The protagonist of this novel imagines a scholarship as referring to him by a slur and telling people to "keep him running."

example.text: This novel ends after Ras the Destroyer sparks a race riot, and it begins with its narrator forced into a "Battle Royale."
For 10 points, name this novel by Ralph Ellison.
Jack leads a group known as the Brotherhood in this novel, which is opposed by the black nationalist Ras the Exhorter.

This novel closes with a riot involving Ras the Exhorter in Harlem, and opens with the title character, who lives in a basement illuminated by over a thousand light bulbs, forced into a "battle royal" with other blacks.
That character, Tod Clifton, was part of an organization in this novel whose enemies include a character who starts a riot in Harlem named Ras the Exhorter.
The narrator of this novel is reminded of Louis Armstrong's song "Black and Blue" while imagining talking to a slave woman mourning her master's death.
A man in this novel decides against using Emma for secret information, opting instead for a drunken woman who fantasizes about being raped, named Sybil.
The narrator of this novel is reminded of Louis Armstrong's song "Black and Blue" while imagining talking to a slave woman mourning her master's death.
This novel's protagonist is shown a card bearing the question "What is your name?" after undergoing electric shock therapy, and narrates this novel from a cellar lit with thousands of light bulbs.
